entry: Petroleum trust (1882–1911) that held a near monopoly on the U.S. oil industry from 1899. Standard Oil Company (Ohio) was founded in 1870 by [[John D. Rockefeller]] and associates, and grew through acquisitions and discounted railroad freight rates. In 1882 its holdings were pooled into a trust of 40 companies valued at $70 million and managed by nine trustees. In 1899 Standard Oil Company of New Jersey became the holding company for the trust and the largest corporation in the United States. In *Standard Oil Co. of New Jersey v. United States* (1911), the Supreme Court found it guilty of anticompetitive practices and ordered it broken up. The severed companies had a net value of $375 million, 57 percent of Jersey Standard's value. Jersey Standard, renamed Exxon in 1973 and ExxonMobil in 1999, remained one of the largest public oil companies. Reporting by Ida Tarbell contributed to the charges.

Unit of pressure (symbol atm) defined as 101325 Pa, approximately equal to Earth's average atmospheric pressure at [[Sea level|sea level]]. Originally defined as the pressure exerted by a 760 mm column of mercury at 0 °C under standard gravity, it was adopted for general use by the 10th General Conference on Weights and Measures in 1954, defined independently of any particular substance. In [[Chemistry|chemistry]], the International Union of Pure and Applied Chemistry recommended in 1982 a standard pressure of exactly 100 kPa (1 bar) for specifying the physical properties of substances. One standard atmosphere equals 760 mmHg, 29.92 inHg and 2116.22 pounds-force per square foot.

Measure of the variation of a set of values about their arithmetic [[Average|average]], used in statistics. A low standard deviation means the values cluster near the average; a high one means they are spread over a wider range. It is most often represented by the Greek letter σ (sigma) and equals the [[Square root|square root]] of the [[Variance|variance]], so it is expressed in the same unit as the data. For a [[Normal distribution|normal distribution]], about 68.3% of values fall within one standard deviation of the average, 95.4% within two and 99.7% within three. It can also be used to calculate the [[Standard error|standard error]] for a finite sample and to determine statistical significance.

Standard deviation of the sampling distribution of a statistic, equal to the square root of the variance of an estimator. The standard error of the mean equals the standard deviation divided by the square root of the sample size. Because the population standard deviation is seldom known, it is usually estimated by substituting the sample standard deviation. The standard error is often used in calculating [[Confidence interval|confidence intervals]] and also appears in [[Regression analysis|regression analysis]]. Small samples tend to underestimate the population standard deviation: with n = 2 the underestimate is about 25%, and with n = 6 only 5%. Reducing the error by a factor of two requires four times as many observations.

Reference conditions for temperature and pressure, used to compare experimental and industrial data, especially gas volumes. The most used standards are those of the International Union of Pure and Applied Chemistry (IUPAC) and the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST), though they are not universally accepted. Since 1982 IUPAC has defined STP as 273.15 K (0.00 °C) and an absolute pressure of exactly 1 [[Bar (unit)|bar]] (100,000.000 Pa); before that it used 1 [[Standard atmosphere (unit)|standard atmosphere]] (101,325.000 Pa). Many technical publications simply say "standard conditions" without specifying them.

Process of developing and implementing technical standards based on consensus among firms, users, interest groups, standards organizations and governments. Standardization can maximize compatibility, interoperability, safety, repeatability, efficiency and quality, and can normalize formerly custom processes. In [[Economics|economics]], it addresses coordination problems in which all parties gain only by making mutually consistent decisions; divergent national standards impose costs on consumers and can act as a non-tariff trade barrier. Standard weights and measures were developed in the Indus Valley, where towns such as [[Mohenjo-daro|Mohenjo-daro]] used uniform units of length. The [[Industrial Revolution|Industrial Revolution]] made standards highly important for machine tools and [[Interchangeable parts|interchangeable parts]]; in 1800 Henry Maudslay's screw-cutting lathe allowed screw-thread sizes to be standardized for the first time.

Private research university in Stanford, California, founded in 1885 by railroad magnate Leland Stanford and his wife, Jane, in memory of their only child, who died of typhoid at age 15. It admitted its first students in 1891 as a coeducational, nondenominational institution. After [[World War II|World War II]], provost Frederick Terman fostered an entrepreneurial culture that gave rise to [[Silicon Valley|Silicon Valley]]; Stanford Research Park, established in Palo Alto in 1951, was the world's first university research park. Organized into seven schools on an 8,180-acre (3,310-hectare) campus, the university houses the Hoover Institution, a public policy think tank. Students and alumni have won 302 Olympic medals, and the university has won 136 NCAA team championships. It is associated with 60 Nobel laureates.

Controversial 1971 psychological experiment at [[Stanford University|Stanford University]]. Run in August 1971 by [[Psychology|psychology]] professor Philip Zimbardo, it was designed as a two-week simulation of prison life. 24 male college students were randomly assigned as prisoners or guards and paid $15 per day. Guards wore uniforms designed to de-individuate them. Abuse of prisoners escalated, and Zimbardo ended the experiment on the sixth day. The study has been widely criticized as unethical and helped prompt stronger review of human research. Thibault Le Texier argued that Zimbardo guided the guards' behavior to confirm conclusions written in advance; Zimbardo disputed the claims.

[[Hong Kong|Hong Kong]] and [[Macau|Macau]] billionaire businessman, nicknamed the Godfather and King of Gambling. He founded SJM Holdings, which owns 19 casinos in Macau, including the Grand Lisboa. Ho held a government-granted monopoly on Macau's gambling industry for 40 years. His business interests spanned entertainment, tourism, shipping, real estate, banking and air transport. After a stroke in July 2009, he began devolving control of his empire to his wives and children from late 2010, including daughter Pansy Ho and son Lawrence Ho.

American filmmaker and photographer of the [[New Hollywood|New Hollywood]] era, regarded as one of the greatest and most influential filmmakers. Born in New York City, he worked as a photographer for *Look* magazine before making his first major Hollywood film, *The Killing* (1956). He settled in England in 1961. At Childwickbury Manor, his home and workplace from 1978, he centralized the writing, editing and management of his productions, giving him almost complete artistic control. His films include *Lolita* (1962), *Dr. Strangelove* (1964) and *A Clockwork Orange* (1971). *2001: A Space Odyssey* (1968) earned him his only [[Academy Awards|Academy Award]], for Best Visual Effects. Known for perfectionism, he often asked for several dozen retakes of a shot.

English footballer who played as an outside right. Often regarded as one of England's greatest players, he was knighted while still playing. He won the inaugural Ballon d'Or in 1956. He spent 19 years at Stoke City and 14 years at Blackpool, where he helped win the 1953 FA Cup in the "Matthews final." He won 54 caps for England between 1934 and 1957, playing in the [[FIFA World Cup|World Cup]] in 1950 and 1954. In 1975 he established an all-black team in Soweto, South Africa, known as "Stan's Men," despite [[Apartheid|apartheid]] laws.

Gram-positive, spherical bacterium (*Staphylococcus aureus*) that is a usual member of the human microbiota, found in the nostrils and on the [[Skin|skin]]. Estimates suggest 21% to 30% of people are long-term carriers. Although usually a commensal, it is an opportunistic pathogen and a common cause of skin infections, abscesses and food poisoning, and it can cause life-threatening [[Pneumonia|pneumonia]], [[Meningitis|meningitis]] and [[Sepsis|sepsis]]. It is one of the five most common causes of hospital-acquired infections; around 500,000 hospital patients in the United States contract a staphylococcal infection each year, chiefly from *S. aureus*. Up to 50,000 deaths a year in the U.S. are linked to staphylococcal infection. Methicillin-resistant *S. aureus* (MRSA) is a leading pathogen in deaths associated with antimicrobial resistance, and no [[Vaccine|vaccine]] has been approved.

American [[Science fiction|science fiction]] media franchise created by [[Gene Roddenberry|Gene Roddenberry]] and owned by Paramount. It began with the series *Star Trek*, which premiered on September 6, 1966, on Canada's CTV network and on [[NBC|NBC]] in the United States on September 8. The series follows the crew of the starship USS Enterprise on a mission "to explore strange new worlds, to seek out new life and new civilizations." The franchise has expanded into films, television series, video games, novels and comic books, and is among the highest-grossing media franchises of all time. Its original series included one of the first multiracial casts on American television, and the franchise is noted for progressive stances on civil rights. Fans are called "Trekkies" or "Trekkers," and the constructed language Klingon was created for it.

American [[Science fiction|science fiction]] television series created by [[Gene Roddenberry|Gene Roddenberry]], the third series in the [[Star Trek|Star Trek]] franchise. Syndicated from September 28, 1987, to May 23, 1994, it ran 178 episodes over seven seasons. Set in the late 24th century, it follows the crew of the starship USS Enterprise (NCC-1701-D), with [[Patrick Stewart|Patrick Stewart]] as Captain Jean-Luc Picard. The show reached almost 12 million viewers in its fifth season. It received 19 Emmy Awards, two Hugo Awards and one Peabody Award, and a Lifetime Achievement Award for the entire cast in 2024.

American [[Science fiction|science fiction]] television series created by [[Gene Roddenberry|Gene Roddenberry]]. It follows the starship USS Enterprise (NCC-1701) and its crew, led by Captain James T. Kirk ([[William Shatner|William Shatner]]), set in the Milky Way, c. 2266–2269. It aired on [[NBC|NBC]] from September 8, 1966, to June 3, 1969, and was canceled after three seasons and 79 episodes because of low ratings. Syndication later made it an international success and a cult classic. It was first shown in the United Kingdom on July 12, 1969, on BBC One, coinciding with the [[Apollo 11|Apollo 11]] Moon landing.

American media franchise created by [[George Lucas|George Lucas]], a space opera saga that began with the 1977 film *Star Wars*. It includes films, television series, video games, novels, comic books, theme park attractions and an all-encompassing fictional universe. A prequel trilogy written and directed by Lucas was followed by a sequel trilogy made after Lucas sold his production company to Disney in 2012. The Force, a mystical energy field, and the conflict between the Jedi peacekeepers and the dark-side Sith are central to the stories, which unfold in a galaxy of rebellions, republics and empires. The theatrical live-action films have grossed over $10 billion, making it the third-highest-grossing film franchise in cinematic history.

1977 American space opera film written and directed by [[George Lucas|George Lucas]] and the first in the *Star Wars* franchise. It stars [[Mark Hamill|Mark Hamill]], [[Harrison Ford|Harrison Ford]] and [[Carrie Fisher|Carrie Fisher]] in a Rebel Alliance campaign against the Galactic Empire's Death Star. Filming began in March 1976 in [[Tunisia|Tunisia]] and at Elstree Studios in England. Released in a small number of U.S. theaters on May 25, 1977, it became a surprise blockbuster. Its total gross reached $775 million with reissues. It received six [[Academy Awards|Academy Awards]], and it entered the National Film Registry in 1989.

Group of stars that share an origin, formed at roughly the same time and held together by self-gravitation. Globular clusters are tight groups of ten thousand to millions of old stars that remain gravitationally bound for billions of years. Open clusters are looser groups, generally containing fewer than a few hundred members, that are young because [[Molecular cloud|giant molecular clouds]] disrupt them over time. Once no longer bound, they become stellar associations, or moving groups. Star clusters visible to the naked eye in the [[Milky Way|Milky Way]] include the [[Pleiades|Pleiades]] and [[Hyades (star cluster)|Hyades]] open clusters and the globular cluster 47 Tucanae. Clusters obscured in visible light but seen in [[Infrared|infrared]] light are classified as infrared clusters.

Process by which dense regions within [[Molecular cloud|molecular clouds]] in interstellar space collapse to form stars, sometimes called stellar nurseries. As a branch of astronomy, it studies the [[Interstellar medium|interstellar medium]] and giant molecular clouds as precursors, and protostars and young stellar objects as products. Most stars form in groups called [[Star cluster|star clusters]] or stellar associations, and star formation theory must account for [[Binary star|binary stars]] and the initial mass function. Filaments in molecular clouds fragment into gravitationally bound cores, most of which evolve into stars. Giant molecular clouds, typically with densities of 100 particles per cm³, can have diameters of 100 light-years and masses of up to 6 million [[Solar mass|solar masses]]; the coldest clouds tend to form low-mass stars.

Hexagram symbol generally recognized as representing Jewish identity and [[Judaism|Judaism]], formed by two equilateral triangles. Its use as a distinctive symbol of the [[Jews|Jewish people]] dates to 17th-century [[Prague|Prague]], and it spread through Jewish communities in Eastern Europe in the 19th century. It became representative of [[Zionism|Zionism]] when chosen as the central symbol of a Jewish national flag at the First Zionist Congress in 1897. By the end of [[World War I|World War I]] it was an internationally accepted symbol of the Jewish people, and it is the central symbol on the national flag of Israel.

Small number of stars that orbit each other, bound by gravitational attraction. A system of two stars is a [[Binary star|binary star]]; systems of three or four are called ternary or quaternary, and systems with four or more components are rare. Most multiple-star systems are hierarchical, with nested orbits that do not interact much, and each level can be treated as a two-body problem. Binary and multiple stars make up about a third of the star systems in the [[Milky Way|Milky Way]], with two-thirds of stars being single. Examples of binary systems include [[Sirius|Sirius]], [[Procyon|Procyon]] and [[Cygnus X-1|Cygnus X-1]], which consists of a star and a [[Black hole|black hole]]. Star systems are smaller than open [[Star cluster|star clusters]], which typically have 100 to 1,000 stars.

American multinational coffeehouse chain headquartered in [[Seattle|Seattle]], Washington. It was founded in 1971 by Jerry Baldwin, Zev Siegl and Gordon Bowker at Seattle's Pike Place Market, initially as a coffee bean wholesaler. Under Howard Schultz, chief executive from 1986 to 2000, it was converted into a coffee shop serving espresso-based drinks and expanded aggressively. As of November 2022 it had 35,711 stores in 80 countries, making it the world's largest coffeehouse chain. Depending on the country, most locations offer [[Wi-Fi|free Wi-Fi]]. The company has been subject to multiple controversies over its business practices.

Galaxy undergoing an exceptionally high rate of star formation, compared with its long-term average or with most other galaxies. The [[Milky Way|Milky Way]] forms about 3 [[Solar mass|solar masses]] of stars per year, while starburst galaxies can experience rates of 100 solar masses per year or more. Because the gas is consumed so quickly, a starburst is typically a brief phase in a galaxy's evolution. The majority of starbursts are in a merger or close encounter with another galaxy. Starbursts are defined by a birthrate parameter of 3 or more, and they make up about 1% of star-forming galaxies in the local universe. Examples include M82 and the Antennae Galaxies (NGC 4038/NGC 4039).

Glucose polymer produced by most green plants for energy storage. It is a [[Carbohydrate|carbohydrate]] of numerous [[Glucose|glucose]] units joined by glycosidic bonds, and the most common carbohydrate in human diets. Major sources include staple foods such as wheat, potatoes, [[Maize|maize]] (corn), rice and [[Cassava|cassava]]. Starch is a white, tasteless, odorless powder insoluble in cold water or alcohol. It consists of two molecules: the linear, helical amylose, usually 20–25% of the starch, and the branched amylopectin. Animals store a more highly branched version, [[Glycogen|glycogen]]. Industrially, starch is converted into sugars that are fermented into ethanol for [[Beer|beer]], [[Whisky|whisky]] and biofuel. Mixed with warm water, most starches form a paste used as a thickening or gluing agent and as the main adhesive in papermaking.

2016 farm life simulation video game developed by Eric "ConcernedApe" Barone. Players inherit their late grandfather's run-down [[Farm|farm]] and restore it by clearing land, growing seasonal [[Crop|crops]] and raising animals, while building relationships with townspeople. Barone developed the game alone over five years, inspired by the Harvest Moon series. The British studio Chucklefish offered to publish it halfway through development. Released for [[Microsoft Windows|Windows]] in February 2016, it was later ported to consoles and mobile devices. It had sold 50 million copies by February 2026.
